facts.text: Otello premiered at La Scala, Milan, on 5 February 1887 and was a resounding success.
facts.evidence: When it finally premiered in Milan on 5 February 1887, it proved to be a resounding success

facts.text: The first-night audience called Verdi back for 20 curtain calls at the end of the opera.
facts.evidence: The audience's enthusiasm for Verdi was shown by the 20 curtain calls that he took at the end of the opera.

facts.text: After Aida (1871) Verdi retired from opera. It took his publisher Ricordi about ten years to coax him into even looking at Boito’s libretto.
evidence: The composer was reluctant to write anything new after the success of Aida in 1871, and he retreated into retirement.
It took his Milan publisher Giulio Ricordi the next ten years

facts.text: For three Christmases in a row Ricordi sent Verdi a cake topped with a chocolate figure of the Moor. The secret project was nicknamed “chocolate”.
evidence: send a cake to Verdi with the figure of the Moor—in chocolate—on the top
the name given to the project for many years, "chocolate"

facts.text: Boito proposed Iago’s “a sort of evil Credo”. Verdi’s verdict: “Most beautiful this Credo; most powerful and wholly Shakespearian.”
evidence: he immediately proposes "a sort of evil Credo
Most beautiful this Credo; most powerful and wholly Shakespearian

facts.text: With “Esultate!” Verdi “hit upon the precise form of one of the most famous entrances in all opera.”
facts.evidence: hit upon the precise form of one of the most famous entrances in all opera" – Otello's "Esultate"

facts.text: Preparations for the premiere were held in absolute secrecy, and Verdi kept the right to cancel it up to the last minute.
facts.evidence: preparations for the initial performance were conducted in absolute secrecy and Verdi reserved the right to cancel the premiere up to the last minute

facts.text: Verdi only settled on the title in a letter to Boito: “I would find it hypocritical not to call it Otello.”
facts.evidence: I would find it hypocritical not to call it Otello.

facts.text: Enrico Caruso was studying Otello when he died in 1921, ending the Met’s plans to stage it for its star tenor.
facts.evidence: Enrico Caruso was studying Otello when he died unexpectedly in 1921, thus thwarting the New York Metropolitan Opera company's plans

facts.text: Plácido Domingo: when he decided to sing Otello, “many people told me that I was crazy” because his voice was nothing like Mario Del Monaco’s.
facts.attribution: Plácido Domingo, My First Forty Years (via Wikipedia)
evidence: When I decided to sing Otello, many people told me that I was crazy
Mario Del Monaco, they said, had had the proper kind of voice for the role

facts.text: Even the first Otello, Francesco Tamagno, didn’t fully satisfy Verdi: a letter to his publisher says Tamagno “left a great deal to be desired”.
facts.evidence: the composer makes it quite clear that Tamagno left a great deal to be desired

facts.text: For years white singers wore dark makeup as Otello. The Met stopped the practice in 2015.
evidence: For many years it was common for white singers to wear dark makeup when playing Otello.
The Metropolitan Opera stopped the practice in 2015.
